title: Zero Returns to Compulsory Schooling in Germany: Evidence and Interpretation
research_question: What is the causal effect of an additional year of compulsory secondary schooling on subsequent labor market earnings in West Germany? Does extending mandatory schooling also affect employment, self-employment, choice of secondary school track, and participation in post-secondary apprenticeship or vocational training?
data_description: The analysis combines three West German micro datasets covering cohorts born 1930-1960 in the ten West German states (excluding Berlin). The Qualification and Career Survey (QaC), a repeated cross-section of employed German nationals aged 15-65 collected by IAB and BIBB, provides waves 1979, 1985-86, 1991-92, and 1998-99 (about 25,000 workers each) with detailed schooling, training, secondary graduation year, bracketed gross monthly earnings, and job-skill use. The Micro Census, an annual 1% household survey (1989, 1991, 1993, 1995-2001; 300,000-400,000 West German observations per wave), provides bracketed net monthly income, employment, and self-employment status. The IAB Employee Sample, a 1% social security panel for 1975-1995, supplies cell-level means/medians of gross earnings (truncated at the social security cap) by year, age, state, and schooling (12,566 cells from ~2.4 million records). Key variables include constructed years of education, length of schooling, log hourly wage, track attended, and an indicator for whether a cohort's state had introduced the 9th grade.
institutional_context: After World War II, West Germany's tracked secondary school system channeled roughly 75% of students into the basic track (Hauptschule), which originally ended at grade 8. Education policy is set by individual Länder within national framework agreements, and starting with Hamburg and Berlin in 1949, states gradually added a compulsory 9th grade to the basic track. The reform diffused unevenly across the ten West German states, with Schleswig-Holstein and Bremen adopting in the late 1950s, Niedersachsen and Saarland in the early 1960s, four states in 1967 following the 1964 Hamburg Accord, and Bavaria not until 1970. Roughly 60% of students attended the affected basic track, after which most entered a regulated apprenticeship system overseen by chambers of commerce and crafts, with nationally agreed curricula and union-negotiated allowances. Because tracking occurs around age 10-11 and apprenticeship lengths were unchanged, the reform isolates a marginal extra year of lower-secondary schooling for predominantly lower-ability students.
